title: Children Bring Higher Meaning and Purpose to Life
author: Stephen Cranney
summary: Stephen Cranney asks whether parents really find more meaning in life, given evidence that daily happiness often dips with young children at home. He separates hedonic pleasure from eudaimonic well-being, the sense of purpose and worth, and tests the latter in the US data of the Baylor/Harvard Global Flourishing Study for adults aged 18 to 39. Both men and women with children are more likely to say they understand their purpose and that their activities are worthwhile, and the effect rises with number of children up to about two for women and three for men. Childless adults score lowest. The relationship survives controls for religion and demographics, though part of the effect reflects that parents are more likely to be married and religious. He lists corroborating studies from Europe and Finland and concludes the conventional wisdom is empirically supported.
points: Parents' lower hedonic happiness and higher eudaimonic meaning can both be true, so measuring purpose rather than pleasure changes the verdict on parenthood.
Among Americans aged 18 to 39, men and women with children report more life purpose, and the benefit rises up to two children for women and three for men.
Childless adults are the least likely to say their activities are worthwhile.
Part of the effect is explained by marriage and religiosity, but meaning remains significant after statistical controls.
A Finnish longitudinal study found purpose rising around the time children arrive, which strengthens the causal reading.
quotes: Conventional wisdom holds that children bring a special kind of existential purpose into the lives of their parents.

If happiness is viewed in terms of what is known as hedonic pleasure—the pleasures of life like sleep, spare time, and fun out on the town—then it makes sense that children can feel like a net negative.
So, do parents under 40 have more purpose and meaning in their life than those with fewer or no children? The answer is clearly yes—for both men and women.
Both men and women are increasingly likely to say they understand their purpose in life as their number of children increases (up to 2 children for women and up to three children for men).
For both men and women, those who have no children are the least likely to say that the things they do in life are worthwhile.

A Finnish study measured the same people across time (a very robust design), and found within people that their sense of purpose increased right before and during the early stages of having children before stabilizing.
Children, while expensive in many ways, tend to contribute a higher meaning to their parents’ lives not already provided by the typical pleasures of life.
